1	# TAC-6 · Let Your Agents Focus — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 57:16 · Advanced (first of three) · Tactic #6: **One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose**
4	> Lesson artifact: the tac-6 codebase — the Natural Language SQL app wrapped in a five-step agentic layer. New this lesson: `/review`, `/patch`, `/document`, `conditional_docs.md`, `prepare_app.md`, seven new ADW scripts, and the Cloudflare R2 uploader.
5	
6	**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** Finish the software developer lifecycle — review (is what we built what we asked for? prove it) and document (how does it work, and when should future agents read about it?) — with dedicated one-purpose agents, because a fresh focused context window per step beats one polluted god-session every time.
7	
8	**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## Idea 1 — The SDLC is five questions, and two were still unanswered
13	
14	**Hook.** After five lessons your agents can plan, build, and test. Dan opens with a claim: with just those three steps "you will outperform any cloud-based agentic coding tool." So why are there two more lessons of machinery? Because your agents still can't answer two questions: *did we build what was asked?* and *how does it work?*
15	
16	**Picture.** Frame t0152 (2:32): the SDLC-as-Questions slide — 1 Plan / 2 Build / 3 Test / 4 Review / 5 Document with all five questions, and Review's carries a suffix no other step has: **"(Prove it)"**.
17	
18	**Worked example.** The question framing is executable: each question is one ADW script and one prompt. `adws/adw_plan.py`→`/chore|/bug|/feature`, `adw_build.py`→`/implement`, `adw_test.py`→`/test`, `adw_review.py`→`/review`, `adw_document.py`→`/document`. The lesson's composers are literally sentences made of questions: `adw_plan_build_review.py`, `adw_sdlc.py`.
19	
20	**Dan's term.** *SDLC as questions and answers.* "The plan step asks, what are we building? The build step asks, did we make it real? Testing says, does it work? The review step asks, is what we built what we planned. And then of course, document asks, how does it work?"
21	
22	**Failure mode.** Treating the five steps as ceremony instead of as a question checklist. The test: for any workflow you own, can you name the question each stage answers? If two stages answer the same question, one of them is redundant; if a question has no stage, you have a hole — most teams' hole is exactly review-as-distinct-from-testing.
23	
24	**Retrieval Q.** State the five questions, and which step demands proof. *(What are we building / did we make it real / does it work / is what we built what we planned — prove it / how does it work.)*
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Idea 2 — Review ≠ testing: different questions, different agents
29	
30	**Hook.** "Some engineering teams group these together. I think that's a massive mistake, especially in the age of agents." The whole demo is engineered to make this distinction bite: a feature that *works* (testing would pass the download) and still isn't *what was asked* (the button is in the wrong place).
31	
32	**Picture.** Frame t1912 (31:52): the review's own uploaded screenshot showing the Export button floating mid-header instead of "directly to the left of the 'hide' button" — the spec line the issue highlighted.
33	
34	**Worked example.** `review.md` says it in bold: "we're not testing. We know the functionality works. We're reviewing the implementation against the spec to make sure it matches what was requested." It reads the spec from `specs/`, diffs against `origin/main`, uses `.claude/commands/e2e/test_*.md` files **only as navigation guides** for where to screenshot, and returns spec-conformance findings — not test results, not code-quality notes ("we're handing all that off to our agents").
35	
36	**Dan's term.** *Review answers: is what we built what we asked for?* Also *review velocity* — the KPI this step exists to raise.
37	
38	**Failure mode.** Two directions: (a) merging review into CI ("tests pass = reviewed") — the demo's bug sails through; (b) letting review re-litigate code quality and architecture — that's not its question, and it burns the focused window on someone else's job.
39	
40	**Retrieval Q.** The demo feature downloaded a correct CSV. Why did review still have work to do? *(It answers a different question: the placement requirement in the spec was violated even though functionality worked.)*
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Idea 3 — Tactic #6: One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose
45	
46	**Hook.** "This tactic drives great agentic development at scale because it forces us to make a controversial decision and commit to it." The controversy: while big tech chases the all-in-one god model, you go the other way — many small agents, each with one committed prompt and one purpose.
47	
48	**Picture.** Frame t0278 (4:38): the tactic slide — definition paragraph plus five Daily Actions (dedicated agents per workflow step; prompts focused on single purposes; free up context windows; commit and version-control all agent prompts; evaluate and improve individual agent performance).
49	
50	**Worked example.** The codebase enforces it structurally: every phase constructs an `AgentTemplateRequest` with a named agent and exactly one slash command. `adw_review.py` declares its cast as constants at the top — `AGENT_REVIEWER = "reviewer"`, `AGENT_REVIEW_PATCH_PLANNER`, `AGENT_REVIEW_PATCH_IMPLEMENTOR` — and no agent runs a second prompt, ever. Search `slash_command=` and you get all 14 call sites in 4 files: the complete inventory of what any agent can be asked to do.
51	
52	**Dan's term.** *One agent, one prompt, one purpose* — "one, one, one." Crucial nuance kept verbatim: "this doesn't mean the prompt isn't large or the prompt doesn't do a lot of work" — the prompts are template meta prompts and higher-order prompts from lessons 3–5.
53	
54	**Failure mode.** Reading "one purpose" as "simple prompts" and gutting the templates; or nodding along and then stacking plan+build+review into one interactive mega-session "to save tokens" — which quietly rebuilds the god-session the tactic exists to kill.
55	
56	**Retrieval Q.** What's the strongest one-sentence proof the tactic is real in this codebase, and what does the tactic NOT mean? *(No agent runs more than a single prompt; it does not mean prompts are small — purpose is singular, work is not.)*
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Idea 4 — Context pollution and the minimum context principle
61	
62	**Hook.** "Isn't more context better for your agent? The more it knows the better it performs?" Dan's answer is flat: "This is not true." He gives the failure a name you'll recognize in your own sessions: a distracted, confused agent that's lost track of the original task.
63	
64	**Picture.** No slide — this run (4:55–11:20) is deliberately talking-head. Render as a designed spread: one polluted 1M-token window vs five fresh windows, each holding only its step's context. (Frame plan flags this beat `diagram_instead`.)
65	
66	**Worked example.** The tactic's payoff in numbers Dan names: "you give your agent the full 200K, 500K, 1 million tokens... all of the space and the opportunity to solve the one problem well." And the codebase's implementation of *minimum context*: prompts declare variables at the top (`adw_id: $1`, `spec_file: $2`...) that act as "information dense keywords on the fly," referenced throughout; `conditional_docs.md` loads documentation **only** when a condition matches — "You don't want to excessively read documentation."
67	
68	**Dan's term.** *Context pollution / context overloading / toxic context*; *the minimum context principle* ("context engineer as little as possible"); *adopt your agent's perspective*. The three constraints: context window, codebase+problem complexity, your abilities — "specialized agents bypass two out of three." And the guardrail: "model intelligence is not a constraint... this is a losing mindset."
69	
70	**Failure mode.** Cargo-culting context: pasting the whole repo, every doc, every prior transcript into each prompt "to be safe." Every added token is another variable the agent must reason about. Second failure: leaning on `/compact` to survive bloated sessions — "if your agent is running compact, it is losing information." The band-aid is not the cure.
71	
72	**Retrieval Q.** Name the three constraints, the two the tactic bypasses, and what Dan calls compact. *(Context window / complexity / abilities; bypasses window + abilities; compact is a band-aid fix that loses information.)*
73	
74	---
75	
76	## Idea 5 — Committed prompts become evals
77	
78	**Hook.** A side effect of one-one-one that Dan flags as "a big idea" he won't fully explore: because every step is a committed prompt file with reproducible state, **your codebase becomes evaluable**.
79	
80	**Picture.** Frame t1305's right half (data_types.py) plus the model map: `/review`→opus, `/document`→sonnet — per-step model routing in eight lines of `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP`.
81	
82	**Worked example.** The eval loop with tools you already have: `git checkout` the state before a run, change one variable (model in the map, thinking mode, agentic tool), rerun `uv run adws/adw_review.py 14 <adw-id>`, diff the two `ReviewResult` JSONs. In-loop runs "battle test" prompts until they're ready to run out-loop in the AFK system. Passive version: you'll form evals in your head just by watching which prompts work.
83	
84	**Dan's term.** *Evals for the agentic layer of your codebase.* Supporting: "we can easily reproduce and more importantly, improve every single step down to the prompt level," vs. others "running big context windows that'll be blown away at the end."
85	
86	**Failure mode.** Prompt archaeology: iterating prompts inside chat history, where nothing is committed, nothing reruns, and improvements evaporate. If you can't `git log` your agent's behavior change, you don't have an agentic layer — you have vibes.
87	
88	**Retrieval Q.** What two properties make a workflow step evaluable, and name two knobs you can turn between runs. *(Committed prompt + reproducible state; model per slash command / thinking mode / agentic tool.)*
89	
90	---
91	
92	## Idea 6 — The review ADW: typed proof, severity triage, agentic resolution
93	
94	**Hook.** "Whenever you want to understand one of these workflows, go right to the main method." The review workflow's docstring already tells the story: find spec → review against it → screenshot critical paths → resolve issues → post results → push and update the PR.
95	
96	**Picture.** Frame t1305 (21:45): review.md's Output Structure beside the `ReviewResult`/`ReviewIssue` pydantic types — the prompt contract and the code type are the same shape. Frame t1068 (17:48): the 7-line `adw_state.json` that chains every phase.
97	
98	**Worked example.** The pipeline, exactly as coded in `adw_review.py`: adw-id **required** → load state, checkout the state's branch → `find_spec_file` (state → diff → branch-pattern glob) → init `R2Uploader` (silently disabled unless all four Cloudflare vars exist) → up to `MAX_REVIEW_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3`: run `/review` (opus), parse strict JSON into `ReviewResult` (a parse failure synthesizes a *blocker* — the pipeline fails loud) → upload screenshots to `adw/{adw_id}/review/…`, save URLs into state for the documenter → post the grouped report (🚨/⚠️/ℹ️ + raw JSON payload) → if blockers: patch-and-re-review; finally commit, push, update PR; exit 1 if blockers remain. The prompt side: 1–5 numbered screenshots (`01_name.png`), critical paths only, absolute paths, `prepare_app.md` executed first (reset DB, background start).
99	
100	**Dan's term.** *Severity guidelines* — `skippable` / `tech_debt` / `blocker`; "we don't want to block on skippable or tech debt." And the warning that motivates them: "these agents are very agreeable... if you ask them to find something, they'll find something. You want to give them the tools to delineate what is important."
101	
102	**Failure mode.** No triage contract → every nitpick blocks the release. No typed output → downstream code parses prose. No retry cap → the loop fixes forever. Each guardrail in this file answers a specific agent pathology; strip one and you rediscover the pathology.
103	
104	**Retrieval Q.** Which severities block, what caps resolution, and what happens when the review output fails to parse? *(Only blockers; 3 attempts; a synthetic blocker-severity ReviewResult — loud failure.)*
105	
106	---
107	
108	## Idea 7 — The patch loop: surgical fixes, reused implementor
109	
110	**Hook.** The review's proof exposed a real bug (Export not left of Hide). Watch what Dan does *not* do: he doesn't open the CSS. He writes a comment containing `adw_patch` and runs a workflow — "I'm going to operate this like we're working outside the loop just for good practice."
111	
112	**Picture.** Frame t2190 (36:30): the whole patch run in one terminal — plan at `specs/patch/patch-adw-490eb6b5-fix-download-button-position.md`, commit `patch: fix button layout for export feature`, comments to issue #14, PR #15 updated, "Patch workflow completed successfully." Frame t2255 (37:35): Export now sitting immediately left of Hide.
113	
114	**Worked example.** `/patch` is a template meta prompt like chore/bug/feature — but its class is different: "we're just changing one thing. We want a simple quick fix." Minimal scope ("Address only the `review_change_request`"), 2–5 steps, validation pulled from the spec or `test.md`, a lines-of-code estimate and risk level. Then `create_and_implement_patch()` validates the returned path (`specs/patch/*.md`) and hands it to the same `/implement` higher-order prompt every other plan uses. Note the on-camera stumble worth teaching: Dan first passed 15 (the PR number) instead of issue 14 — the state echo in the issue comments is how you catch it.
115	
116	**Dan's term.** *Patch* as a distinct problem class; *create and implement patch* as the shared method; "we're starting to get some reuse of the compositional pieces of our code base."
117	
118	**Failure mode.** "Why didn't you just do that by hand?" — Dan pre-empts it: "You're missing the point... we are putting in the effort to build the system that builds the system... This isn't about you anymore. It's about teaching your agents how to build on your behalf, so that it can be about you again." Hand-fixes leave the system exactly as fallible as before.
119	
120	**Retrieval Q.** How is a standalone patch triggered, and which prompt implements the patch plan? *(The literal keyword `adw_patch` in the latest issue comment or body, then `uv run adws/adw_patch.py <issue> [adw-id]`; the reused `/implement` higher-order prompt.)*
121	
122	---
123	
124	## Idea 8 — Document: two problems, and the loop that closes the SDLC
125	
126	**Hook.** "Documentation is simple, but how you document and when to include your documentation is the tricky part." Two problems, two mechanisms — and the second one is the lesson's finale: it makes the whole lifecycle a loop.
127	
128	**Picture.** Frame t2742 (45:42): `conditional_docs.md` with the fifth entry the documenter just appended (`app_docs/feature-490eb6b5-one-click-table-exports.md` — "When working with CSV export functionality"). Frame t2815 (46:55): search proof that bug, chore, document, feature, patch, and prime all reference conditional docs.
129	
130	**Worked example.** `adw_document.py` (adw-id required; graceful skip when `git diff origin/main` is empty) passes `[adw_id, spec_path, screenshots_dir]` to `/document`, which: analyzes the diff (--stat, --name-only, per-file for >50-line changes), reads the spec, copies review screenshots into `app_docs/assets/`, writes `app_docs/feature-{adw_id}-{name}.md` from the committed template (Overview → Screenshots → What Was Built → Technical Implementation → How to Use → Configuration → Testing → Notes), **then updates `conditional_docs.md`** and returns exclusively the doc path. Committed baseline: exactly 4 conditional entries; the fifth appears only after your documenter runs. Taxonomy note kept verbatim: "AI docs for third party, app docs is for your codebase."
131	
132	**Dan's term.** *Conditional documentation*; *the agentic layer feedback loop*: "our agents are fully connected, right, from planning to building to testing to reviewing to documenting their work... This seals the deal. This connects them all." Caveat he states: the conditional pattern relies on model strength — "if they just come in here and read them... scale up your model."
133	
134	**Failure mode.** Docs written for humans only, stored where no prompt looks, or bulk-loaded into every prompt (pollution again). Also hand-editing `conditional_docs.md` — the entry must be the documenter's job or the loop has a human SPOF.
135

156	## Idea 10 — Presence, proof, and the KPI scoreboard
157	
158	**Hook.** The lesson ends by grading itself. One prompt shipped a real feature — and the scoreboard still shows dents. That honesty is the point: the KPIs tell you where your agentic layer needs work, not how to feel.

Generalization for non-UI folks, kept explicit: scikit classifiers, data analytics, rapid prototypes — "whatever you would do to review that the thing is what you asked for... this is what you're going to embed into your review step," and it should yield a *hard asset*, ideally "a live asset" (report, image, video).

Plus the bridge out: lesson 7 reveals "the secret of Tactical Agentic Coding... hiding in plain sight throughout TAC," and dangerous-mode ADWs shipping to production — "not for serious work... maybe some bugs, maybe some chores." And the closing order: "do not wait to start putting this stuff in your codebase."

166	**Failure mode.** Reading KPIs as vanity metrics or, worse, gaming them (never patching so attempts stays 1). The scoreboard is a diagnosis: attempts up → improve the prompt that missed; presence up → move that human moment into a workflow.

# TAC-6 · Let Your Agents Focus — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 57:16 · Advanced (first of three) · Tactic #6: **One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose**
> Lesson artifact: the tac-6 codebase — the Natural Language SQL app wrapped in a five-step agentic layer. New this lesson: `/review`, `/patch`, `/document`, `conditional_docs.md`, `prepare_app.md`, seven new ADW scripts, and the Cloudflare R2 uploader.

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** Finish the software developer lifecycle — review (is what we built what we asked for? prove it) and document (how does it work, and when should future agents read about it?) — with dedicated one-purpose agents, because a fresh focused context window per step beats one polluted god-session every time.

**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.

---

## Idea 1 — The SDLC is five questions, and two were still unanswered

**Hook.** After five lessons your agents can plan, build, and test. Dan opens with a claim: with just those three steps "you will outperform any cloud-based agentic coding tool." So why are there two more lessons of machinery? Because your agents still can't answer two questions: *did we build what was asked?* and *how does it work?*

**Picture.** Frame t0152 (2:32): the SDLC-as-Questions slide — 1 Plan / 2 Build / 3 Test / 4 Review / 5 Document with all five questions, and Review's carries a suffix no other step has: **"(Prove it)"**.

**Worked example.** The question framing is executable: each question is one ADW script and one prompt. `adws/adw_plan.py`→`/chore|/bug|/feature`, `adw_build.py`→`/implement`, `adw_test.py`→`/test`, `adw_review.py`→`/review`, `adw_document.py`→`/document`. The lesson's composers are literally sentences made of questions: `adw_plan_build_review.py`, `adw_sdlc.py`.

**Dan's term.** *SDLC as questions and answers.* "The plan step asks, what are we building? The build step asks, did we make it real? Testing says, does it work? The review step asks, is what we built what we planned. And then of course, document asks, how does it work?"

**Failure mode.** Treating the five steps as ceremony instead of as a question checklist. The test: for any workflow you own, can you name the question each stage answers? If two stages answer the same question, one of them is redundant; if a question has no stage, you have a hole — most teams' hole is exactly review-as-distinct-from-testing.

**Retrieval Q.** State the five questions, and which step demands proof. *(What are we building / did we make it real / does it work / is what we built what we planned — prove it / how does it work.)*

---

## Idea 2 — Review ≠ testing: different questions, different agents

**Hook.** "Some engineering teams group these together. I think that's a massive mistake, especially in the age of agents." The whole demo is engineered to make this distinction bite: a feature that *works* (testing would pass the download) and still isn't *what was asked* (the button is in the wrong place).

**Picture.** Frame t1912 (31:52): the review's own uploaded screenshot showing the Export button floating mid-header instead of "directly to the left of the 'hide' button" — the spec line the issue highlighted.

**Worked example.** `review.md` says it in bold: "we're not testing. We know the functionality works. We're reviewing the implementation against the spec to make sure it matches what was requested." It reads the spec from `specs/`, diffs against `origin/main`, uses `.claude/commands/e2e/test_*.md` files **only as navigation guides** for where to screenshot, and returns spec-conformance findings — not test results, not code-quality notes ("we're handing all that off to our agents").

**Dan's term.** *Review answers: is what we built what we asked for?* Also *review velocity* — the KPI this step exists to raise.

**Failure mode.** Two directions: (a) merging review into CI ("tests pass = reviewed") — the demo's bug sails through; (b) letting review re-litigate code quality and architecture — that's not its question, and it burns the focused window on someone else's job.

**Retrieval Q.** The demo feature downloaded a correct CSV. Why did review still have work to do? *(It answers a different question: the placement requirement in the spec was violated even though functionality worked.)*

---

## Idea 3 — Tactic #6: One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose

**Hook.** "This tactic drives great agentic development at scale because it forces us to make a controversial decision and commit to it." The controversy: while big tech chases the all-in-one god model, you go the other way — many small agents, each with one committed prompt and one purpose.

**Picture.** Frame t0278 (4:38): the tactic slide — definition paragraph plus five Daily Actions (dedicated agents per workflow step; prompts focused on single purposes; free up context windows; commit and version-control all agent prompts; evaluate and improve individual agent performance).

**Worked example.** The codebase enforces it structurally: every phase constructs an `AgentTemplateRequest` with a named agent and exactly one slash command. `adw_review.py` declares its cast as constants at the top — `AGENT_REVIEWER = "reviewer"`, `AGENT_REVIEW_PATCH_PLANNER`, `AGENT_REVIEW_PATCH_IMPLEMENTOR` — and no agent runs a second prompt, ever. Search `slash_command=` and you get all 14 call sites in 4 files: the complete inventory of what any agent can be asked to do.

**Dan's term.** *One agent, one prompt, one purpose* — "one, one, one." Crucial nuance kept verbatim: "this doesn't mean the prompt isn't large or the prompt doesn't do a lot of work" — the prompts are template meta prompts and higher-order prompts from lessons 3–5.

**Failure mode.** Reading "one purpose" as "simple prompts" and gutting the templates; or nodding along and then stacking plan+build+review into one interactive mega-session "to save tokens" — which quietly rebuilds the god-session the tactic exists to kill.

**Retrieval Q.** What's the strongest one-sentence proof the tactic is real in this codebase, and what does the tactic NOT mean? *(No agent runs more than a single prompt; it does not mean prompts are small — purpose is singular, work is not.)*

---

## Idea 4 — Context pollution and the minimum context principle

**Hook.** "Isn't more context better for your agent? The more it knows the better it performs?" Dan's answer is flat: "This is not true." He gives the failure a name you'll recognize in your own sessions: a distracted, confused agent that's lost track of the original task.

**Picture.** No slide — this run (4:55–11:20) is deliberately talking-head. Render as a designed spread: one polluted 1M-token window vs five fresh windows, each holding only its step's context. (Frame plan flags this beat `diagram_instead`.)

**Worked example.** The tactic's payoff in numbers Dan names: "you give your agent the full 200K, 500K, 1 million tokens... all of the space and the opportunity to solve the one problem well." And the codebase's implementation of *minimum context*: prompts declare variables at the top (`adw_id: $1`, `spec_file: $2`...) that act as "information dense keywords on the fly," referenced throughout; `conditional_docs.md` loads documentation **only** when a condition matches — "You don't want to excessively read documentation."

**Dan's term.** *Context pollution / context overloading / toxic context*; *the minimum context principle* ("context engineer as little as possible"); *adopt your agent's perspective*. The three constraints: context window, codebase+problem complexity, your abilities — "specialized agents bypass two out of three." And the guardrail: "model intelligence is not a constraint... this is a losing mindset."

**Failure mode.** Cargo-culting context: pasting the whole repo, every doc, every prior transcript into each prompt "to be safe." Every added token is another variable the agent must reason about. Second failure: leaning on `/compact` to survive bloated sessions — "if your agent is running compact, it is losing information." The band-aid is not the cure.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the three constraints, the two the tactic bypasses, and what Dan calls compact. *(Context window / complexity / abilities; bypasses window + abilities; compact is a band-aid fix that loses information.)*

---

## Idea 5 — Committed prompts become evals

**Hook.** A side effect of one-one-one that Dan flags as "a big idea" he won't fully explore: because every step is a committed prompt file with reproducible state, **your codebase becomes evaluable**.

**Picture.** Frame t1305's right half (data_types.py) plus the model map: `/review`→opus, `/document`→sonnet — per-step model routing in eight lines of `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP`.

**Worked example.** The eval loop with tools you already have: `git checkout` the state before a run, change one variable (model in the map, thinking mode, agentic tool), rerun `uv run adws/adw_review.py 14 <adw-id>`, diff the two `ReviewResult` JSONs. In-loop runs "battle test" prompts until they're ready to run out-loop in the AFK system. Passive version: you'll form evals in your head just by watching which prompts work.

**Dan's term.** *Evals for the agentic layer of your codebase.* Supporting: "we can easily reproduce and more importantly, improve every single step down to the prompt level," vs. others "running big context windows that'll be blown away at the end."

**Failure mode.** Prompt archaeology: iterating prompts inside chat history, where nothing is committed, nothing reruns, and improvements evaporate. If you can't `git log` your agent's behavior change, you don't have an agentic layer — you have vibes.

**Retrieval Q.** What two properties make a workflow step evaluable, and name two knobs you can turn between runs. *(Committed prompt + reproducible state; model per slash command / thinking mode / agentic tool.)*

---

## Idea 6 — The review ADW: typed proof, severity triage, agentic resolution

**Hook.** "Whenever you want to understand one of these workflows, go right to the main method." The review workflow's docstring already tells the story: find spec → review against it → screenshot critical paths → resolve issues → post results → push and update the PR.

**Picture.** Frame t1305 (21:45): review.md's Output Structure beside the `ReviewResult`/`ReviewIssue` pydantic types — the prompt contract and the code type are the same shape. Frame t1068 (17:48): the 7-line `adw_state.json` that chains every phase.

**Worked example.** The pipeline, exactly as coded in `adw_review.py`: adw-id **required** → load state, checkout the state's branch → `find_spec_file` (state → diff → branch-pattern glob) → init `R2Uploader` (silently disabled unless all four Cloudflare vars exist) → up to `MAX_REVIEW_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3`: run `/review` (opus), parse strict JSON into `ReviewResult` (a parse failure synthesizes a *blocker* — the pipeline fails loud) → upload screenshots to `adw/{adw_id}/review/…`, save URLs into state for the documenter → post the grouped report (🚨/⚠️/ℹ️ + raw JSON payload) → if blockers: patch-and-re-review; finally commit, push, update PR; exit 1 if blockers remain. The prompt side: 1–5 numbered screenshots (`01_name.png`), critical paths only, absolute paths, `prepare_app.md` executed first (reset DB, background start).

**Dan's term.** *Severity guidelines* — `skippable` / `tech_debt` / `blocker`; "we don't want to block on skippable or tech debt." And the warning that motivates them: "these agents are very agreeable... if you ask them to find something, they'll find something. You want to give them the tools to delineate what is important."

**Failure mode.** No triage contract → every nitpick blocks the release. No typed output → downstream code parses prose. No retry cap → the loop fixes forever. Each guardrail in this file answers a specific agent pathology; strip one and you rediscover the pathology.

**Retrieval Q.** Which severities block, what caps resolution, and what happens when the review output fails to parse? *(Only blockers; 3 attempts; a synthetic blocker-severity ReviewResult — loud failure.)*

---

## Idea 7 — The patch loop: surgical fixes, reused implementor

**Hook.** The review's proof exposed a real bug (Export not left of Hide). Watch what Dan does *not* do: he doesn't open the CSS. He writes a comment containing `adw_patch` and runs a workflow — "I'm going to operate this like we're working outside the loop just for good practice."

**Picture.** Frame t2190 (36:30): the whole patch run in one terminal — plan at `specs/patch/patch-adw-490eb6b5-fix-download-button-position.md`, commit `patch: fix button layout for export feature`, comments to issue #14, PR #15 updated, "Patch workflow completed successfully." Frame t2255 (37:35): Export now sitting immediately left of Hide.

**Worked example.** `/patch` is a template meta prompt like chore/bug/feature — but its class is different: "we're just changing one thing. We want a simple quick fix." Minimal scope ("Address only the `review_change_request`"), 2–5 steps, validation pulled from the spec or `test.md`, a lines-of-code estimate and risk level. Then `create_and_implement_patch()` validates the returned path (`specs/patch/*.md`) and hands it to the same `/implement` higher-order prompt every other plan uses. Note the on-camera stumble worth teaching: Dan first passed 15 (the PR number) instead of issue 14 — the state echo in the issue comments is how you catch it.

**Dan's term.** *Patch* as a distinct problem class; *create and implement patch* as the shared method; "we're starting to get some reuse of the compositional pieces of our code base."

**Failure mode.** "Why didn't you just do that by hand?" — Dan pre-empts it: "You're missing the point... we are putting in the effort to build the system that builds the system... This isn't about you anymore. It's about teaching your agents how to build on your behalf, so that it can be about you again." Hand-fixes leave the system exactly as fallible as before.

**Retrieval Q.** How is a standalone patch triggered, and which prompt implements the patch plan? *(The literal keyword `adw_patch` in the latest issue comment or body, then `uv run adws/adw_patch.py <issue> [adw-id]`; the reused `/implement` higher-order prompt.)*

---

## Idea 8 — Document: two problems, and the loop that closes the SDLC

**Hook.** "Documentation is simple, but how you document and when to include your documentation is the tricky part." Two problems, two mechanisms — and the second one is the lesson's finale: it makes the whole lifecycle a loop.

**Picture.** Frame t2742 (45:42): `conditional_docs.md` with the fifth entry the documenter just appended (`app_docs/feature-490eb6b5-one-click-table-exports.md` — "When working with CSV export functionality"). Frame t2815 (46:55): search proof that bug, chore, document, feature, patch, and prime all reference conditional docs.

**Worked example.** `adw_document.py` (adw-id required; graceful skip when `git diff origin/main` is empty) passes `[adw_id, spec_path, screenshots_dir]` to `/document`, which: analyzes the diff (--stat, --name-only, per-file for >50-line changes), reads the spec, copies review screenshots into `app_docs/assets/`, writes `app_docs/feature-{adw_id}-{name}.md` from the committed template (Overview → Screenshots → What Was Built → Technical Implementation → How to Use → Configuration → Testing → Notes), **then updates `conditional_docs.md`** and returns exclusively the doc path. Committed baseline: exactly 4 conditional entries; the fifth appears only after your documenter runs. Taxonomy note kept verbatim: "AI docs for third party, app docs is for your codebase."

**Dan's term.** *Conditional documentation*; *the agentic layer feedback loop*: "our agents are fully connected, right, from planning to building to testing to reviewing to documenting their work... This seals the deal. This connects them all." Caveat he states: the conditional pattern relies on model strength — "if they just come in here and read them... scale up your model."

**Failure mode.** Docs written for humans only, stored where no prompt looks, or bulk-loaded into every prompt (pollution again). Also hand-editing `conditional_docs.md` — the entry must be the documenter's job or the loop has a human SPOF.

**Retrieval Q.** What TWO artifacts does the document step produce/modify, and who reads the second one? *(`app_docs/feature-…md` + an appended `conditional_docs.md` entry; read by bug, chore, feature, patch, and prime at planning time.)*

---

## Idea 9 — When review misses: blame the layer, upgrade the layer

**Hook.** The uncomfortable twist: the review step *itself* failed here — the spec said "directly to the left of the hide button," the plan carried it, the agent missed it, and the review report said success. Dan's response is the lesson's most transferable posture: "I'm not blaming the model for this. I'm blaming my skills. I'm blaming the ADWs we have set up right now."

**Picture.** Frame t2135 (35:35): `.mcp.json` with `--vision` typed in — and then rejected ("I don't like this because this is outside of the ADW... keep general configuration here").

**Worked example.** The post-mortem, exactly as run on camera: (1) the test step was **skipped** — `adw_plan_build_review`, not `adw_plan_build_test_review`; "the UI test very likely would have caught this... this is probably the winning workflow." (2) The reviewer captures screenshots it never reads — no vision flow; "the actual screenshots never make it into the agent. The tokens aren't flowing through the vision capabilities of our language model." The fix he chooses belongs in the *prompt*, not the global config: "for every image you take, be sure to read it in during the review process." (3) Verify the chain before blaming a link: was the requirement in the issue? yes. In the plan? yes ("did I have the original request inside the plan... let's just look"). So the gap is review's — now you know *which* prompt to improve.

**Dan's term.** *Fix the end-to-end portion, not the thing that went wrong.* "If something goes wrong, you fix the end to end portion... They're called out-loop systems for a reason."

**Failure mode.** Model-blaming (a losing mindset, and it points you at the one thing you can't fix) — or its mirror, silently hand-patching the artifact and leaving the review prompt exactly as blind as it was. The failure *class* must land in the layer: a prompt instruction, a workflow choice, a template line.

**Retrieval Q.** Give both root causes for the missed placement bug and Dan's chosen fix location. *(Test step skipped; screenshots never read into context — fix goes into the review prompt's instructions, not .mcp.json.)*

---

## Idea 10 — Presence, proof, and the KPI scoreboard

**Hook.** The lesson ends by grading itself. One prompt shipped a real feature — and the scoreboard still shows dents. That honesty is the point: the KPIs tell you where your agentic layer needs work, not how to feel.

**Picture.** Designed scoreboard (no frame — 54:55–56:10 is talking head): Attempts 1→2 (the patch). Size: solid (two endpoints, two UI surfaces, tests, plan, docs — "a couple of prompts, we have 900 lines of code of engineering work"). Streak: broken, reset to 1 (two ADWs for one feature). Presence: ~3 (prompt input; spotting the issue in the review images; patch + re-check) vs the ideal 2 — "one at the beginning for your prompt input, one at the end for your review and your PR merge."

**Worked example.** What made presence cheap even when needed: the review system carried proof to *you* — "we were able to quickly identify this issue thanks to our review images and just patch it." Generalization for non-UI folks, kept explicit: scikit classifiers, data analytics, rapid prototypes — "whatever you would do to review that the thing is what you asked for... this is what you're going to embed into your review step," and it should yield a *hard asset*, ideally "a live asset" (report, image, video).

**Dan's term.** *Agentic proof of value*; *review velocity*; *live asset*. Plus the bridge out: lesson 7 reveals "the secret of Tactical Agentic Coding... hiding in plain sight throughout TAC," and dangerous-mode ADWs shipping to production — "not for serious work... maybe some bugs, maybe some chores." And the closing order: "do not wait to start putting this stuff in your codebase."

**Failure mode.** Reading KPIs as vanity metrics or, worse, gaming them (never patching so attempts stays 1). The scoreboard is a diagnosis: attempts up → improve the prompt that missed; presence up → move that human moment into a workflow.

**Retrieval Q.** Ideal presence is what number, at which two moments — and what does an attempts increase tell you to do? *(2: prompt input, review/PR merge; improve the workflow/prompt whose miss forced the extra attempt.)*

---

## Timeline map (VTT-verified)

| Time | Beat |
|---|---|
| 0:00–2:10 | Advanced-lesson open: review + document complete the SDLC; fleet-of-agents future; "outperform any cloud-based agentic coding tool" |
| 2:10–3:00 | **SDLC as questions** slide; testing-vs-review distinction; "prove it" |
| 3:00–3:40 | Review velocity; KPIs: attempts down, streak up, size up, presence down |
| 3:40–4:20 | Why document: feedback for future agents inside the agentic layer |
| 4:20–4:55 | **Tactic #6 reveal: One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose** |
| 4:55–7:10 | Context pollution; god-model critique ("they won't, it's not here"); ADWs = compute added to YOUR developer workflows; steps need different context |
| 7:10–8:30 | Free the window (200K/500K/1M); three constraints (bypass 2/3); model intelligence not a constraint; compact = band-aid |
| 8:30–10:04 | Let your agents focus; minimum context principle; agent's perspective; commit prompts → improve at prompt level |
| 10:04–11:20 | Evals for the agentic layer (deep + passive); "one, one, one" |
| 11:20–12:30 | Clone tac-6; YOLO mode + Opus; `/install` (+ Cloudflare R2 teaser) |
| 12:30–13:40 | New ADWs tour: review/patch/document + composers; standalone UV scripts; ADW ID chains state |
| 13:40–15:30 | adw_review docstring read; fork-your-own-repo note; `/start`; app back up |
| 15:30–16:47 | Issue #14 "One Click Table Exports" (prompt source; high-level drifting mid-level) |
| 16:47–18:40 | Fire `adw_plan_build_review.py … 14`; agents own the repo; `agents/{id}/` + `adw_state.json` |
| 18:40–23:00 | Review deep-dive: R2 uploader; `/review` prompt (variables as IDKs, screenshots, JSON contract); ReviewResult/ReviewIssue types; severity classes; agreeable-agents warning |
| 23:00–27:30 | Resolution: 3-attempt cap; blockers only; `/patch` meta prompt; `create_and_implement_patch`; `/implement` reuse |
| 27:30–31:40 | Progress checks; branch changed under him; `git diff --stat origin/main` (plan + generated e2e test); R2 enabled |
| 31:41–33:30 | **Review lands with images**; the misplaced Export exposed; "our agent did not obey this properly" |
| 33:30–35:20 | Click-through: downloads work, placement wrong; post-mortem part 1: test step skipped |
| 35:20–37:45 | Post-mortem part 2: no vision — screenshots never read; prompt-level fix; `adw_patch` comment → patch run → **"Export is now right next to hide"** |
| 37:45–42:30 | "Why didn't you do it by hand? You're missing the point"; CSV verified; out-loop patching via webhook; commander-of-compute callback |
| 42:30–45:30 | `adw_document.py` on same ADW ID; `app_docs/feature-490eb6b5-…md` + assets; doc template; stale screenshot noted (review not rerun) |
| 45:30–48:00 | **Conditional docs**: agentic update; referenced in bug/chore/feature/patch/prime; "this seals the deal" |
| 48:00–53:30 | Issue/PR recap (~900 lines); agents present proof; blame-my-ADWs posture; non-UI review embodiments; live asset |
| 53:30–57:16 | Toy-example disclaimer; velocity teaser; **secret of TAC** teaser; KPI self-grade (attempts 2, streak reset, presence ~3, ideal 2); dangerous-mode teaser; "do not wait" |

## Terminology glossary (Dan-isms, canonical spellings)

- **One agent, one prompt, one purpose** — Tactic #6; no agent runs more than a single prompt
- **Context pollution / context overloading / toxic context** — degraded focus from an overloaded window
- **Minimum context principle** — context engineer as little as possible; minimum context required to solve the problem
- **Three constraints** — context window; codebase+problem complexity; your abilities (model intelligence deliberately excluded)
- **SDLC as questions** — plan/build/test/review/document ↔ their five questions
- **Review velocity** — how fast a human can say yes/no; raised by proof
- **Severity classes** — `skippable` / `tech_debt` / `blocker` (only blockers block)
- **Patch** — a surgical change class distinct from chore/bug/feature
- **Conditional documentation** — docs indexed by read-me-when conditions; updated by the documenter, read by planners
- **app_docs vs ai_docs** — your codebase's docs vs third-party docs
- **Agentic proof of value / live asset** — hard evidence attached to review (image/video/report)
- **Presence** — human-in-the-loop moments per shipped unit; ideal = 2
- **PITER** — Prompt, Input, Trigger, Environment, Review (TAC-4 framework; transcript mishears as "Peter")
- Transcript corrections: "yellow mode" → YOLO mode, "AWID" → ADW ID, "loop box" → loot box, "Huffactor" → (mishear; he's booting the agent)

- Constant thread made explicit here: the value isn't any single workflow — "it's the power of combining workflows, having them separate yet working together... isolated... reviewable... improvable"
- Standing order: "do not wait to start putting this stuff in your codebase. Set up basic ADWs, set up basic agentic prompts... the value here is immense"

1	# TAC-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner
2	
3	Ordering rule: how much of the rest of the course breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you motivated and honest.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else
8	
9	**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
10	AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
11	*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?
12	
13	**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
14	Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
15	*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."
16	
17	**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
18	The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.
19	
20	**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
21	`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Tier 2 — The working machinery
26	
27	**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
28	Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.

# TAC-1 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of the rest of the course breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you motivated and honest.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. The whole upgrade is ONE added ingredient.**
AI coding runs on the big three: **context, model, prompt**. Agentic coding = big three + **tools**, and "tools" means *prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls*. That's the core four. Every lesson after this one is just scaling that fourth ingredient.
*Why weak learners lose it:* it sounds too small to matter. Test yourself: when a run fails, can you name which of the four was wrong?

**2. Stop coding ≠ stop shipping code, and ≠ stop reading code.**
Stop *typing* it. Agents type; you plan, review, and build closed loops. Code volume goes UP; your keystrokes go to zero. If you hand-edit the agent's file when it's 90% right instead of re-prompting, you've quietly quit the course.
*Say it Dan's way:* "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code. Full stop."

**3. A prompt can BE a workflow.**
The README's agentic prompt isn't a request for text — it's a runbook: RUN (branch) → CREATE (file) → RUN (execute, add, commit). The agent plans it as a checklist and does engineering work. If you can only remember one artifact from the lesson, remember what those 12 lines did.

**4. The agent is a function you can call from code.**
`claude -p "<prompt>"` from shell, Python, or TypeScript. Three tiny scripts in `programmable/` prove it. This is the seed of everything "systems that build systems" means — the agent stops being a chat window and becomes a building block you can embed anywhere, including places you aren't.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. The A/B test is the lesson. Run it, don't watch it.**
Same repo, two prompts: `main_aic.py` (file generated — phase 1) vs branch+file+runs+commit+report (engineering done — phase 2). Then delete the branch and rerun it *headlessly* with `uv run python programmable/programmable.py`. Feeling the rerun is what installs the concept.

**6. Read `.claude/settings.json` before you run anything. Always.**
It's the agent's entire tool surface: Read/Write/Edit, `uv run`, four git commands, WebSearch. Know what the agent MAY do and you can predict everything it will do. This habit scales to every agentic tool you'll ever touch.

**7. "Tool calling isn't new" — correct, and irrelevant.**
Dan's rebuttal, verbatim: "It's not a question of new. It's a question of **scale and performance**." What's new is *reliable long chains*: plans that survive twelve consecutive tool calls without derailing.

**8. Why Claude Code (three essential elements).**
(1) A model that can reason when needed, (2) consistent long tool chains, (3) the right agent architecture. Together they made "reliable agentic coding at scale" possible for the first time. Use the trio as a checklist for judging ANY agentic tool — that's the transferable part. Don't get stuck on any one tool.

**9. Make the agent REPORT.**
`programmable/prompt.md` ends with `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. Headless work you can't verify is work you can't trust. Report-back is the first closed-loop habit of the course.

**10. Wrapped in the right tool, prompts become long-running workflows.**
Minutes to hours, end to end, with and without your oversight — fired repeatedly with the right triggers at the right time. That's the scale Dan is asking you not to turn your brain off about.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you going

**11. You're an engineer, not a coder.**
Engineering was never about writing code; it's about systems of leverage that produce outcomes for users and customers. This reframe is what makes Tactic #1 survivable emotionally.

**12. 10x comes from leverage, never from effort.**
And the number is arbitrary — 2x, 10x, 100x — set by the leverage points you find. 80% of life is noise and repetition; this is the rare opportunity worth focusing on.

**13. Pay to play.**
Millions and millions of tokens across the course. Budget for it (plan or API funds) or you'll stall mid-lesson and blame the tactics.

**14. The contradicting truth: to become irreplaceable, replace yourself.**
Whoever automates the work owns the automation. What gets replaced is your typing; what becomes irreplaceable is your judgment and your ownership of the systems doing the work.

**15. The mission has named enemies.**
"An engineer *they* can't replace — your boss, the company, the industry, AI." Nothing in tech is forever; constant evolution is the price of staying valuable. That's why lesson 1 spends six minutes on stakes before touching a terminal.

---

## Micro-quiz (close the book first)

1. Big three? Core four? Which element is new and what's its precise definition?
2. Five things the agentic prompt did that the AI coding prompt didn't?
3. What file tells you the agent's tool surface, and what's in it here?
4. Write the shell version of the programmable pattern from memory (3 lines).
5. What does prompt.md's REPORT block demand, and why does that matter for headless runs?
6. Resolve the paradox: how does replacing yourself make you irreplaceable?

*(Answers: extract.md ideas 4, 5, 4/6, 7, 7, 8.)*

1	# TAC-1 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)
2	
3	TAC-1 ages unusually well because it teaches primitives, and Dan future-proofs on camera: *"Your Claude Code UI might look different. You might be using newer models. That's all great... Don't let that distract you from the value embedded in each lesson."* Still, five things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Reusable agent behavior: prompt files → Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap
8	
9	**Course era:** reusable behavior is encoded as a raw prompt file (`programmable/prompt.md`) plus launcher scripts. Works, but discovery, triggering, and composition are all manual.
10	**Current:** Agent Skills are the first-class encoding — `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand by Claude Code and shareable across projects/teams. Skills are the modern answer to "how do I package the thing my agent knows how to do?" — exactly the question `programmable/` answers primitively.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. This is the course's most-cited gap ("Skills as modern encoding of engineering"). Teach prompt.md first (pedagogically perfect: no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
12	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
13	
14	## 2. Embedding: bare `claude -p` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `claude -p "<prompt>"` via subprocess from sh/ts/py; output captured as plain text; REPORT requested inside the prompt itself.
17	**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the best teaching form), but production embedding now uses headless flags — `--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume — and, for real systems, the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): structured outputs, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. What TAC-1 calls "programmable agentic coding" grew into a supported product surface.
18	**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the 3-line script you just wrote has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite — concept unchanged: agent as callable component.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
20	
21	## 3. Permissions: flat allowlist → modes, hooks, sandboxing
22	
23	**Course era:** `.claude/settings.json` with a flat `permissions.allow` list (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, four git patterns, `WebSearch`).
24	**Current:** that syntax still works, but the surface grew: permission modes (plan/accept-edits/etc.), pre/post tool-use hooks, sandboxed bash, deny rules, and settings layering (user/project/local). Teams gate agents with hooks, not just allowlists.
25	**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout. The lesson's HABIT — always read what the agent may do before running it — transfers unchanged and is the actual teaching point.
26	**Overlay:** none needed.
27	
28	## 4. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled by Dan
29	
30	**Course era:** course-era Claude models and TUI; Aider cited as the phase-1 analogue.
31	**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
32	**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.
33	
34	## 5. Scale: one serial loop → fleets, subagents, parallel worktrees
35	
36	**Course era:** one agent, one workflow, serially, in one terminal — deliberately, since it's lesson 1 of 8.
37	**Current:** the same agentic prompt is routinely fanned out: subagents, background tasks, git-worktree-isolated parallel runs, orchestrated pipelines. "Systems that build systems" now has industrial-strength machinery.
38	**Book treatment:** forward-pointer only ("the course scales this in later lessons; today's ceiling is higher still"). Overlaying scale content on lesson 1 would front-run the pedagogy.
39	**Overlay candidates (deferred to later chapters):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity*; `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (both include_in_phase1: **no**).
40	
41	---
42	
43	## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)
44	
45	- The phase-1/phase-2 frame and "AI coding is not enough" — if anything, more consensus now than at recording.
46	- The core four. Context/model/prompt/tools remains the complete diagnostic vocabulary for agentic failures.
47	- The agentic prompt as workflow-specification (RUN/CREATE/RUN/REPORT) — this shape is now everywhere (slash commands, skills, CI prompts).
48	- "Scale and performance, not novelty" as the right lens on tool calling.
49	- The three-essential-elements checklist for evaluating agentic tools.
50	- Terminal ubiquity as the embedding superpower.
51	- Report-back as the first closed-loop habit.
52	- The economics: token spend as pay-to-play. (Costs shifted; the logic didn't.)
53	
54	## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3)
55	
56	| # | Video | Maps to | Include |

58	| 1 | `2TIXl2rlA6Q` — AI Coding is NOT ENOUGH | operationalizes tactic (lesson thesis, phase model) | ✅ |
59	| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (form factor + programmable embedding, current state) | ✅ |
60	| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (skills gap) | ✅ |
61	| 4 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | self-operating vision → later lessons | ❌ defer |
62	| 5 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | context engineering → later lessons | ❌ defer |

221	  "quotes": [
222	    { "text": "We nearly arrive at the future where you can run a single prompt that triggers a fleet of agents that ship your work end to end.", "approx_timestamp": "0:28" },
223	    { "text": "Testing answers the question, does it work? But review answers the question, is what we built what we asked for?", "approx_timestamp": "2:24" },
224	    { "text": "We want attempts down, streak up, size up, presence down.", "approx_timestamp": "3:18" },
225	    { "text": "Documentation provides feedback on work done for future agents to reference in their work.", "approx_timestamp": "3:52" },
226	    { "text": "The tactic is one agent, one prompt, one purpose.", "approx_timestamp": "4:33" },
227	    { "text": "Massive context windows often leads to a distracted, confused, agent. This is context pollution. This is context overloading. This is toxic context.", "approx_timestamp": "4:51" },
228	    { "text": "Real engineering requires real developer workflows, not some pie in the sky God model that claims to do it all. And, you know, let me just spoil it for you. They won't. It's not here. It's not coming soon.", "approx_timestamp": "6:21" },
229	    { "text": "You give your agent the full 200K, 500K, 1 million tokens... you give your agent all of the space and the opportunity to solve the one problem well.", "approx_timestamp": "7:13" },
230	    { "text": "As agentic engineers, we have three constraints: the context window, the complexity of our codebase and the problem we're solving, and lastly our abilities. Specialized agents bypass two out of three of these.", "approx_timestamp": "7:34" },
231	    { "text": "Model intelligence is not a constraint. Don't use this as an excuse. It will set you back. This is a losing mindset.", "approx_timestamp": "7:50" },
232	    { "text": "The compact command inside of Claude Code... this is a bandaid fix. If your agent is running compact, it is losing information.", "approx_timestamp": "8:06" },
233	    { "text": "A focused engineer working on a single task is a productive engineer. Agents are the same... When your agent's performance drops, your performance drops. So let your agents focus.", "approx_timestamp": "8:30" },
234	    { "text": "You want to context engineer as little as possible. You want the minimum context in your prompt required to solve the problem.", "approx_timestamp": "8:54" },
235	    { "text": "You effectively create evals for the agentic layer of your codebase.", "approx_timestamp": "10:04" },
236	    { "text": "Everything comes down to the prompt level. All the ADW surrounding deterministic code is just support for the agents doing the real work.", "approx_timestamp": "20:16" },
237	    { "text": "These agents are very agreeable, but they're also just great at engineering... if you ask them to find something, they'll find something. You want to give them the tools to delineate what is important.", "approx_timestamp": "22:26" },
238	    { "text": "You don't want your agents bothering you. You want to reduce the number of human in the loop points there are in your workflow.", "approx_timestamp": "24:40" },
239	    { "text": "They're called out-loop systems for a reason. You want your agent shipping end to end. And if something goes wrong, you fix the end to end portion, not the thing that went wrong.", "approx_timestamp": "25:10" },
240	    { "text": "Why didn't you just do that by hand? You're missing the point... we are putting in the effort to build the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "37:30" },
241	    { "text": "This isn't about you anymore. This is about your agents. It's about teaching your agents how to build on your behalf, so that it can be about you again.", "approx_timestamp": "37:41" },
242	    { "text": "Our agents are fully connected, right, from planning to building to testing to reviewing to documenting their work. It's all connected now. This seals the deal. This connects them all.", "approx_timestamp": "47:39" },
243	    { "text": "Review answers the critical question: is what we built what we asked for? Even when your agent is wrong, when it presents you with proof that it thinks it's right, you can quickly say yes or no.", "approx_timestamp": "50:50" },
244	    { "text": "I'm not blaming the model for this. I'm blaming my skills. I'm blaming the ADWs we have set up right now.", "approx_timestamp": "50:30" },
245	    { "text": "What you want is a live asset that you can review that proves that what was built is what was asked for.", "approx_timestamp": "51:51" },
246	    { "text": "Ideally, you want two moments of presence: one at the beginning for your prompt input, one at the end for your review and your PR merge.", "approx_timestamp": "56:03" }

{
  "lesson_key": "tac-6-let-your-agents-focus",
  "title": "Let Your Agents Focus",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 6,
  "level": "Advanced (first of three advanced lessons)",
  "lesson_subtitle": "Agentic Review and Documentation",
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/let-your-agents-focus",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-6-let-your-agents-focus/video/tac-6-let-your-agents-focus.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 3436,
    "duration_display": "57:16"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose",
    "one_liner": "Give every step of the software developer lifecycle its own specialized agent running one committed prompt toward one purpose — a fresh, focused context window beats a bigger, polluted one every time.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It forces a controversial commitment while the rest of the industry runs the other way. Generative-AI companies and big tech chase the all-in-one god model, the super agent that does it all; Dan tells you to bet against that and deliberately fragment your automation into many small single-purpose agents — 'they won't, it's not here, it's not coming soon. The real engineering still must happen.' It also extends Tactic #1 into new territory: stop even the hands-on one-off low-level prompts ('this isn't about you anymore... it's about teaching your agents how to build on your behalf, so that it can be about you again'), and when a fix is trivially yours to make by hand, run the patch workflow anyway — because you're building the system that builds the system, not the fix."
  },
  "mission": "Complete the last two steps of the software developer lifecycle — review and document — so your agents plan, build, test, review, and document end to end. Review makes agents check that what was built is what you asked for, prove it with hard assets (screenshots), and agentically fix blocking gaps; document makes them record what was done and wire it into conditional documentation so every future agent knows what came before. With all five steps you nearly arrive at the future where one prompt triggers a fleet of agents that ship your work end to end — running YOUR AI developer workflows, with your expertise, in your product. Dan's claim: with just plan/build/test 'you will outperform any cloud-based agentic coding tool' — review and document are what push beyond that.",
  "sdlc_question_model": {
    "plan": "What are we building?",
    "build": "Did we make it real?",
    "test": "Does it work?",
    "review": "Is what we built what we planned? (Prove it)",
    "document": "How does it work?",
    "why_review_is_separate": "Some engineering teams group testing and review together; Dan calls that a massive mistake, especially in the age of agents. Testing answers 'does it work?'. Review answers 'is what we built what we asked for?' — validated against the original plan/spec, not against functionality. Review is explicitly NOT about code quality or implementation details (that's handed off to the agents); it is spec conformance plus proof, and it exists to increase your review velocity.",
    "documentation_two_parts": "Documentation is simple; the tricky parts are HOW you document and WHEN to include it. Part 1: after review passes, generate concise docs for the work. Part 2: knowing when to pull documentation into future prompts — solved by conditional documentation inside the agentic layer."
  },
  "kpi_model": {
    "targets": "Attempts down, streak up, size up, presence down (the TAC agentic coding KPIs, recapped from earlier lessons as the reason review + document exist).",
    "lesson_worked_example": "One prompt shipped the export feature: attempts started at the optimal 1, then the patch pushed attempts to 2 (not good — but the size shipped by the single prompt was solid: table CSV export + query-result CSV export, endpoints, tests, plan). Streak broke (two ADWs needed for one feature → reset to 1). Presence was ~3 (prompt input, spotting the issue from review images, running the patch, reviewing again). Ideal presence is 2: one at the beginning for prompt input, one at the end for review and PR merge.",
    "review_velocity": "Review's KPI contribution: even when your agent is wrong but presents proof it thinks it's right, you can say yes or no in seconds. A live/hard asset (image, video, report) that proves the work directly increases review velocity."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "sdlc-as-questions",
      "name": "The SDLC as questions and answers",
      "plain_english": "Every step of the software developer lifecycle is a question: Plan — what are we building? Build — did we make it real? Test — does it work? Review — is what we built what we planned? Document — how does it work? If you can name the question a step answers, you can build a dedicated agent to answer it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Every step of the software developer lifecycle can be represented as a question and an answer... Notice testing answers the question, does it work? But review answers the question, is what we built what we asked for?\"",
      "misconception": "That testing and review are the same step with two names. Teams that group them lose the distinct question — and in the age of agents, an agent that proves spec conformance is a different specialist from an agent that proves functionality."
    },
    {
      "id": "one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose",
      "name": "Tactic #6: One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose",

    "(27:30-31:40) Check progress in agents/{adw_id}/ (build phase → review phase); branch changed under him — 'our agent is in full control over this system'; git diff --stat origin/main shows plan, e2e test generated from the plan template, implementation. R2 upload enabled: public bucket ready.",

Fix belongs in the prompt ('for every image you take, be sure to read it in') not the global MCP config.",

It sees the git diff + spec, writes app_docs/feature-490eb6b5-one-click-table-exports.md (concise breakdown, files changed, how to use, screenshots embedded — note the screenshot still shows the pre-patch layout because review wasn't rerun: another named improvement), copying images to app_docs/assets/.",

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "We nearly arrive at the future where you can run a single prompt that triggers a fleet of agents that ship your work end to end.", "approx_timestamp": "0:28" },
    { "text": "Testing answers the question, does it work? But review answers the question, is what we built what we asked for?", "approx_timestamp": "2:24" },
    { "text": "We want attempts down, streak up, size up, presence down.", "approx_timestamp": "3:18" },
    { "text": "Documentation provides feedback on work done for future agents to reference in their work.", "approx_timestamp": "3:52" },
    { "text": "The tactic is one agent, one prompt, one purpose.", "approx_timestamp": "4:33" },
    { "text": "Massive context windows often leads to a distracted, confused, agent. This is context pollution. This is context overloading. This is toxic context.", "approx_timestamp": "4:51" },
    { "text": "Real engineering requires real developer workflows, not some pie in the sky God model that claims to do it all. And, you know, let me just spoil it for you. They won't. It's not here. It's not coming soon.", "approx_timestamp": "6:21" },
    { "text": "You give your agent the full 200K, 500K, 1 million tokens... you give your agent all of the space and the opportunity to solve the one problem well.", "approx_timestamp": "7:13" },
    { "text": "As agentic engineers, we have three constraints: the context window, the complexity of our codebase and the problem we're solving, and lastly our abilities. Specialized agents bypass two out of three of these.", "approx_timestamp": "7:34" },
    { "text": "Model intelligence is not a constraint. Don't use this as an excuse. It will set you back. This is a losing mindset.", "approx_timestamp": "7:50" },
    { "text": "The compact command inside of Claude Code... this is a bandaid fix. If your agent is running compact, it is losing information.", "approx_timestamp": "8:06" },
    { "text": "A focused engineer working on a single task is a productive engineer. Agents are the same... When your agent's performance drops, your performance drops. So let your agents focus.", "approx_timestamp": "8:30" },
    { "text": "You want to context engineer as little as possible. You want the minimum context in your prompt required to solve the problem.", "approx_timestamp": "8:54" },
    { "text": "You effectively create evals for the agentic layer of your codebase.", "approx_timestamp": "10:04" },
    { "text": "Everything comes down to the prompt level. All the ADW surrounding deterministic code is just support for the agents doing the real work.", "approx_timestamp": "20:16" },
    { "text": "These agents are very agreeable, but they're also just great at engineering... if you ask them to find something, they'll find something. You want to give them the tools to delineate what is important.", "approx_timestamp": "22:26" },
    { "text": "You don't want your agents bothering you. You want to reduce the number of human in the loop points there are in your workflow.", "approx_timestamp": "24:40" },
    { "text": "They're called out-loop systems for a reason. You want your agent shipping end to end. And if something goes wrong, you fix the end to end portion, not the thing that went wrong.", "approx_timestamp": "25:10" },
    { "text": "Why didn't you just do that by hand? You're missing the point... we are putting in the effort to build the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "37:30" },
    { "text": "This isn't about you anymore. This is about your agents. It's about teaching your agents how to build on your behalf, so that it can be about you again.", "approx_timestamp": "37:41" },
    { "text": "Our agents are fully connected, right, from planning to building to testing to reviewing to documenting their work. It's all connected now. This seals the deal. This connects them all.", "approx_timestamp": "47:39" },
    { "text": "Review answers the critical question: is what we built what we asked for? Even when your agent is wrong, when it presents you with proof that it thinks it's right, you can quickly say yes or no.", "approx_timestamp": "50:50" },
    { "text": "I'm not blaming the model for this. I'm blaming my skills. I'm blaming the ADWs we have set up right now.", "approx_timestamp": "50:30" },
    { "text": "What you want is a live asset that you can review that proves that what was built is what was asked for.", "approx_timestamp": "51:51" },
    { "text": "Ideally, you want two moments of presence: one at the beginning for your prompt input, one at the end for your review and your PR merge.", "approx_timestamp": "56:03" }
  ],
