  "what_student_must_internalize": [
    "The five SDLC questions — plan: what are we building? build: did we make it real? test: does it work? review: is what we built what we planned (prove it)? document: how does it work? A step you can phrase as a question is a step you can hand to a dedicated agent.",
    "Testing ≠ review. Grouping them is 'a massive mistake, especially in the age of agents' — the demo's misplaced-button bug survived precisely because the test step was skipped and review only checked presence, not placement.",
    "One agent, one prompt, one purpose — no agent runs more than a single prompt; prompts may be huge (template meta prompts, higher-order prompts), but each agent has exactly one job.",
    "Why it works: frees the full context window for the one problem; sidesteps context pollution; bypasses two of the three constraints (context window, your abilities) — and model intelligence is not a constraint, that's a losing mindset.",
    "Compact is a band-aid: if your agent is compacting, it is losing information. Design workflows so no single context has to hold everything.",
    "Committed prompts are reproducible, improvable, and evaluable: search the slash command, open the file, know exactly what the agent sees; change model/thinking/tool, checkout the pre-run state, rerun — evals for your agentic layer.",
    "Review must output a typed contract: strict JSON parsed into ReviewResult, severity triage (skippable/tech_debt/blocker), only blockers block, only blockers auto-resolve, retry capped at 3 — and the report always carries proof (1-5 screenshots, publicly hosted).",
    "Agreeable agents need triage vocabulary: they WILL find something if you ask; the severity classes are templated judgment that keeps nitpicks from blocking releases.",
    "Patches are a distinct class of change (surgical, minimal, review_change_request-driven) with their own meta prompt — and the implementor is the same reused /implement higher-order prompt. Run the patch workflow even when your hands could fix it faster; you're building the system that builds the system.",
    "Documentation is two problems: creating docs (from git diff + spec + review screenshots) and knowing when to load them (conditional_docs.md, read by bug/chore/feature/patch/prime and updated by document). That closes the SDLC feedback loop — future planners read what past documenters wrote.",
    "Out-loop bias: reduce human-in-the-loop points; when something breaks, fix the end-to-end system (prompt/workflow), not just the artifact. When review misses, blame your ADWs and skills, not the model — then encode the fix (e.g., 'read every image you take').",
    "Ideal presence is 2: prompt input at the start, review + PR merge at the end. Everything in this lesson exists to make those the only two moments you're needed."
  ],
  "common_weak_student_failures": [
    "Merging testing and review ('we have CI, review is redundant') — losing the spec-conformance question entirely; the lesson's own bug is the counterexample.",
    "Running plan+build+review+document in one long interactive session to 'save tokens' — recreating exactly the context pollution the tactic eliminates, and losing per-step reproducibility.",
    "Hearing 'one purpose' as 'small prompts' and shrinking templates until they're useless. Purpose is singular; prompts stay industrial (meta prompts, higher-order prompts).",
    "Skipping the severity contract, then wondering why every run fails review — agreeable agents report SOMETHING; without skippable/tech_debt/blocker triage everything looks blocking.",
    "Skipping the test ADW because 'review will catch it' — Dan's own demo proves the opposite; plan_build_test_review is 'probably the winning workflow'.",
    "Hand-fixing the misplaced button instead of running adw_patch — 'you're missing the point'; the system never learns and the fix isn't reproducible.",
    "Forgetting that adw_review.py and adw_document.py REQUIRE the adw-id (they hard-exit without state), or passing the PR number instead of the issue number — Dan did exactly this on camera (15 vs 14); read the state echo in the issue comments.",
    "Expecting screenshots to render on GitHub without the Cloudflare R2 env vars (upload silently disables to local paths), or assuming the review agent SAW its screenshots — course-era it never reads them; that's the named improvement.",
    "Editing conditional_docs.md by hand or treating app_docs as human-only documentation — the loop only closes if the documenter agent maintains the conditional index that planners read.",
    "Reviewing from inside the app instead of from the presented proof — booting the environment for every review is the old way; the point of hard assets is review-from-the-issue."
  ],
  "teach_back_prompt": "Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) the five SDLC questions and why 'is what we built what we asked for?' is a different question from 'does it work?' — use the export-button bug as evidence (which step was skipped, what review caught, what review itself missed and why the screenshots never entered the agent's context); (2) the full review→patch→document pipeline: where the spec comes from, what the /review JSON contract and severity classes are, when resolution fires and what caps it, how /patch reuses /implement, and what /document writes AND updates; (3) why one agent, one prompt, one purpose beats one god-session — context pollution, the three constraints, and how committed one-purpose prompts become evals; finish by tracing the loop: which five prompts read conditional_docs.md, which prompt writes it, and what that means for the next feature you plan.",
  "retrieval_questions": [
    { "q": "State the five SDLC steps as questions.", "a": "Plan: what are we building? Build: did we make it real? Test: does it work? Review: is what we built what we planned (prove it)? Document: how does it work?" },
    { "q": "What's the difference between testing and reviewing, and why does Dan refuse to group them?", "a": "Testing answers 'does it work?'; review answers 'is what we built what we asked for?' — spec conformance with proof, not functionality and not code quality. Grouping them is 'a massive mistake, especially in the age of agents' because they're different questions needing different specialist agents." },
    { "q": "What is Tactic #6, and what's the strongest single-sentence evidence it's already in the codebase?", "a": "One agent, one prompt, one purpose. 'No agent runs more than a single prompt' — every ADW phase spawns a named agent that executes exactly one slash-command template and exits." },
    { "q": "Name the three constraints of agentic engineers and which two the tactic bypasses.", "a": "The context window; the complexity of the codebase + problem; your abilities. Specialized agents bypass the context window (fresh, freed per step) and your abilities (engineering templated into committed prompts). Model intelligence is NOT a constraint — treating it as one is a losing mindset." },
    { "q": "Why does Dan call compact a band-aid?", "a": "If your agent is running compact, it is losing information — compression is lossy. One-purpose agents get fresh windows instead of compacted ones." },
    { "q": "What are the three review severity classes, and which ones block?", "a": "skippable, tech_debt, blocker. Only blockers set success=false, and only blockers get auto-resolved by the patch loop." },
    { "q": "Walk the review resolution loop, including its cap.", "a": "Run /review → parse JSON into ReviewResult → upload screenshots to R2 → post report. If blockers: for each blocker, create a patch plan (/patch) and implement it (/implement), commit, then re-review — up to MAX_REVIEW_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3 total attempts. If nothing resolves, stop; if blockers remain at the end, the workflow exits 1 and you fix the agentic layer for that class of issue." },
    { "q": "Why did the misplaced export button survive review, twice over?", "a": "First, the test step was skipped entirely (plan_build_review, not plan_build_test_review) — the UI test 'very likely would have caught this.' Second, the review agent captures screenshots it never reads: no --vision on Playwright MCP and no read-the-image instruction, so the tokens never flowed through the model's vision capabilities." },
    { "q": "How do you trigger a standalone patch out-loop, and what makes /patch different from /bug or /feature?", "a": "Comment (or write in the issue body) the keyword 'adw_patch' plus the change request, then run uv run adws/adw_patch.py <issue> [adw-id] (or let the webhook fire it). /patch creates a minimal, surgical plan in specs/patch/ scoped to only the review_change_request — a different class of change than chore/bug/feature — then reuses the same /implement higher-order prompt." },
    { "q": "What TWO things does the /document prompt produce or modify, and who consumes each?", "a": "It writes app_docs/feature-{adw_id}-{name}.md (with screenshots copied into app_docs/assets/) for humans AND future agents, and it appends an entry to .claude/commands/conditional_docs.md — which bug, chore, feature, patch, and prime read at planning time. That's the plan↔document feedback loop." },
    { "q": "What is the ADW state file, where does it live, and what fields does it carry?", "a": "agents/{adw_id}/adw_state.json — adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class (review adds review_screenshots; document adds documentation_path). The ADW ID chains the state of all phases together." },
    { "q": "How does the codebase route models per prompt, and which prompts get the big model?", "a": "SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP in adw_modules/agent.py: opus for /implement, /review, /bug, /feature, /patch; sonnet for /chore, /document, tests, classification and git ops; default sonnet. Per-purpose agents make per-step model routing (and eval-style reruns) trivial." },
    { "q": "What's the ideal presence count and what are the two moments?", "a": "Two: one at the beginning for prompt input, one at the end for review and PR merge." },
    { "q": "What proof does review owe you, and what does that do to your KPIs?", "a": "A hard/live asset proving the work matches the ask — 1-5 screenshots here; a report, video, or metrics for non-UI domains. Proof lets you say yes/no in seconds even when the agent is wrong, which directly increases review velocity (and drives presence down)." }

# TAC-6 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of the rest of your agentic layer collapses if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is the tactic and its two load-bearing distinctions; Tier 2 is the machinery that makes review and document real; Tier 3 is the posture that keeps you building systems instead of hand-fixing artifacts.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. One agent, one prompt, one purpose — and "one purpose" does NOT mean "small prompt."**
Each workflow step spawns a fresh named agent that runs exactly one slash-command template and exits. No agent ever runs a second prompt. But the prompts are huge — template meta prompts and higher-order prompts from lessons 3–5. Dan is explicit: "this doesn't mean the prompt isn't large or the prompt doesn't do a lot of work." The purpose is singular; the work is not. Gutting your templates to make them "focused" is the #1 way to misread this lesson.
*Test yourself:* search `slash_command=` in the codebase — 14 hits in 4 files is the complete inventory of what any agent can be asked to do. If you can't produce that list, you don't yet see the tactic.

**2. Review is not testing. Different question, different agent.**
Testing asks "does it work?" Review asks "is what we built what we asked for?" — spec conformance, proved, not functionality and not code quality. Dan: grouping them is "a massive mistake, especially in the age of agents." The whole demo is engineered to make this bite: the export button downloads a perfectly correct CSV (testing would pass) and is still in the wrong place (review's job). If your CI is green and you think you're done, you just skipped a question.

**3. The SDLC is five questions, and a step you can phrase as a question is a step you can hand to an agent.**
Plan — what are we building? Build — did we make it real? Test — does it work? Review — is what we built what we planned (prove it)? Document — how does it work? Each question = one ADW script + one prompt. The composers are literally sentences made of questions: `adw_plan_build_review`, `adw_sdlc`. Only Review carries a suffix no other step has: **"(Prove it)."**

**4. More context is not better. Fresh beats big.**
"Isn't more context better for your agent?" Dan: "This is not true." An overloaded window makes a distracted, confused agent that's lost the original task — context pollution / overloading / toxic context. The cure is never a bigger window; it's a fresh, focused window per purpose, holding the minimum context required to solve the one problem. Every token you add is another variable the agent must reason about.
*Corollary weak learners miss:* context engineering in TAC mostly means WITHHOLDING context, not piling it on.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**5. The review ADW is a typed proof machine, not a vibe check.**

# TAC-6 Lab Spec — Let Your Agents Focus

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-6`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-6.git`). You additionally need a GitHub repo YOU control — issues and PRs are the review system. No external repos, no new machinery beyond the lesson's tools.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. The misplaced button, the docs, the patch — all of it flows through an ADW or Claude Code. If your fingers touch `app/client/src/main.ts`, you've quit the lesson.
**Time box:** 90–120 minutes. Token cost: real, and higher than earlier labs — a full plan→build→review run plus a patch run and a document run, with `/review` on opus. Pay to play; budget for it or you'll stall mid-review and blame the tactic.

---

## 0 · Setup (15 min)

1. Clone the lesson repo: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-6.git && cd tac-6`
2. **Own the review surface:** create your own GitHub repo and point origin at it — `git remote remove origin && git remote add origin <your-repo> && git push -u origin main`. ADW review/patch/document need issues and PRs you control. `gh auth status` must be green.
3. Boot `claude`, run `/install`. Fill `.env` from `.env.sample`: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (required — this is the headless billing path), `CLAUDE_CODE_PATH`, and `export GITHUB_REPO_URL`. Fill `app/server/.env` for the app's own NL→SQL key.
4. **Optional but demo-faithful:** set the four Cloudflare R2 vars (`CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` + R2 access key / secret / bucket) so review screenshots render as images on GitHub. Without them you get local file paths in comments — **that is not an error**; the uploader disables silently by design.
5. Sanity: `uv --version`; `/start`; the app serves at `localhost:5173`; run the five-users query to confirm the NL→SQL app works.

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state what makes review/patch/document different from plan/build/test — they need a repo you own, because their output IS issue comments and PR updates.

## 1 · Reproduce Dan — plan → build → review (25 min)

1. Create GitHub issue **"One Click Table Exports"** in Dan's shape: one-click CSV export for tables AND for query results; two new endpoints; the download button **directly LEFT of the tables' "x" icon** and **directly LEFT of the query results' "hide" button**; an appropriate download icon. (This mid-level detail is deliberate — placement is exactly what review will check.)
2. Fire it and hands off: `uv run adws/adw_plan_build_review.py <issue#>` (no adw-id — one gets created). "Our agents have now taken over this repository. We shouldn't be doing anything alongside them." Do NOT touch the repo while it runs.
3. Watch the machinery, don't interrupt it: `agents/{adw_id}/` fills with per-agent folders; `adw_state.json` carries adw_id / issue_number / branch_name / plan_file / issue_class; most of what scrolls by is the workflow REPORTING to the issue.

**Checkpoint 1:** the run posts a review comment. Read it as a contract, not prose — success flag, `review_summary` (standup-style), 1–5 numbered screenshots (R2 URLs or local paths), severity-grouped issues, and the raw JSON payload at the bottom.

## 2 · Read the review contract (15 min)

1. Open `.claude/commands/review.md` beside `adws/adw_modules/data_types.py`. Confirm the prompt's Output Structure and the `ReviewResult` / `ReviewIssue` pydantic types are the same shape; find the severity `Literal['skippable','tech_debt','blocker']`.
2. Answer in writing, no notes:
   - Which severities set `success=false`? Which get auto-resolved? *(blockers; both.)*
   - What caps the resolution loop? *(`MAX_REVIEW_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3`.)*
   - What happens if the review output fails to parse? *(a synthetic blocker-severity `ReviewResult` — the pipeline fails LOUD.)*
   - What does review use the `e2e/test_*.md` files for? *(navigation guides for WHERE to screenshot — only. It is not testing.)*
3. Spot the on-disk quirk: `review.md` has a `./claude/commands/e2e` path typo (missing the leading dot on `.claude`). Agents tolerate it because the intent is clear; a literal grep won't.

**Checkpoint 2:** you can recite the triage contract and the loud-failure behavior from memory.

## 3 · The patch loop, run out-loop (20 min)

1. Inspect the placement in the running app. If your agent nailed the button position, **plant Dan's deviation deliberately** (via Claude Code, not your editor) so you have a blocker to resolve — the point is to run the loop, not to get lucky.
2. Do NOT open the CSS. Comment on the issue with the literal keyword `adw_patch` + one line: "make sure the download button is just to the left of our hide button."
3. Run it like you're out-loop: `uv run adws/adw_patch.py <issue#> <adw-id>`. **Pass the issue number, not the PR number** — Dan fumbled 15-vs-14 on camera; the state echo in the comments is your check.
4. Verify the receipts: a plan under `specs/patch/patch-adw-{adw_id}-*.md`, the fix visible in the app, the commit, and the existing PR updated.

**Checkpoint 3 (write one sentence):** why run a whole workflow for a one-line CSS nudge you could hand-fix in 10 seconds? *(You're building the system that builds the system; a hand-fix leaves the system as fallible as before and isn't reproducible.)*

## 4 · Document, and watch the loop close (15 min)

1. On the SAME state: `uv run adws/adw_document.py <issue#> <adw-id>`.
2. Verify all three outputs: `app_docs/feature-{adw_id}-*.md`, copied images under `app_docs/assets/`, and a NEW entry appended to `.claude/commands/conditional_docs.md` (the committed file ships with exactly 4; yours makes 5).
3. Prove the loop: search `conditional_docs` — it's referenced in bug, chore, feature, patch, and prime. The planners read what your documenter just wrote.

**Checkpoint 4:** state the plan↔document cycle in one breath — document APPENDS the conditional entry; five planning prompts READ it; the next feature you plan pulls this doc only when its condition matches.

## 5 · Stretch drills (15–40 min, still zero hand-typing)

**S1 — The winning workflow.** Rerun the whole feature on a fresh issue with `adw_plan_build_test_review.py`. Note which phase catches your planted deviation — Dan: "the UI test very likely would have caught this... this is probably the winning workflow."
**S2 — Dan's named improvement (vision).** Via Claude Code, add "For every image you take, be sure to read it in during the review process" to `review.md`. Re-run `adw_review.py` on the same adw-id; compare `ReviewResult`s. Note where the fix does NOT belong: the global `.mcp.json --vision` ("this is outside of the ADW").
**S3 — Evals in practice.** Flip `/review` to a different model in `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP`, `git checkout` the pre-review state, rerun, diff the two review JSONs. You just built an eval from git.
**S4 — One-one-one census.** `ls agents/{adw_id}/` after a full run; map every agent folder to its single slash command and one purpose. Confirm no agent ran two prompts.
**S5 — Trigger-drift hunt.** From `classify_adw.md` vs `data_types.ADWWorkflow` / `workflow_ops.AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS`, prove why a webhook can never launch `adw_plan_build_review`. This is prompt↔code contract drift — exactly the failure class a review step exists to catch. (Optional: fix it via an `adw_patch` issue.)

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere — every change flowed through an ADW or Claude Code
- [ ] `agents/{adw_id}/adw_state.json` shows adw_id / issue_number / branch_name / plan_file / issue_class populated across phases
- [ ] Review posted a JSON-backed report with 1–5 screenshots and severity-classified issues
- [ ] You can state which severities block and what caps the resolution loop (3), no notes
- [ ] A patch plan exists under `specs/patch/` and its fix is visible in the app + PR
- [ ] An `app_docs/feature-*.md` exists with copied assets AND `conditional_docs.md` gained its entry **agentically**, not by hand
- [ ] Oral, no notes: five SDLC questions; testing-vs-review distinction; three constraints + which two the tactic bypasses; why compact is a band-aid; ideal presence count and its two moments

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall:** running `adw_review.py` / `adw_document.py` without the adw-id — they hard-exit demanding prior state. Remind students the ADW ID chains everything; copy it from the plan-phase output.
- **Second stall (Dan's own):** passing the PR number instead of the issue number to `adw_patch.py` (15 vs 14). Teach reading the state echo in the issue comments before blaming the tool.
- **"My screenshots are just file paths — it's broken."** No — the R2 uploader disables silently without the four Cloudflare vars. Local paths are the expected fallback; set the vars only if you want images to render on GitHub.
- **"Review passed but the button's wrong — the model failed."** Reframe it exactly as Dan does: blame the ADWs and skills, not the model. Two causes (test skipped; screenshots never read), one fix location (the review prompt). This is the lesson's most important teaching moment — don't let it slide into model-blaming.
- **Cost anxiety:** this lab spends more than TAC-1 (opus review + multiple full ADW runs). If the budget conversation surfaces, that IS the pay-to-play lesson arriving on schedule.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** webhook/cron out-loop triggering at scale, dangerous-mode production ADWs, the fleet-of-agents endgame — those are lesson 7+. Keep the five-question SDLC crisp and deflect scope creep.

3. Run it like you're out-loop: `uv run adws/adw_patch.py <issue#> <adw-id>`. **Pass the issue number, not the PR number** — Dan fumbled 15-vs-14 on camera; the state echo in the comments is your check.
4. Verify the receipts: a plan under `specs/patch/patch-adw-{adw_id}-*.md`, the fix visible in the app, the commit, and the existing PR updated.

**Checkpoint 3 (write one sentence):** why run a whole workflow for a one-line CSS nudge you could hand-fix in 10 seconds? *(You're building the system that builds the system; a hand-fix leaves the system as fallible as before and isn't reproducible.)*

## 4 · Document, and watch the loop close (15 min)

1. On the SAME state: `uv run adws/adw_document.py <issue#> <adw-id>`.
2. Verify all three outputs: `app_docs/feature-{adw_id}-*.md`, copied images under `app_docs/assets/`, and a NEW entry appended to `.claude/commands/conditional_docs.md` (the committed file ships with exactly 4; yours makes 5).
3. Prove the loop: search `conditional_docs` — it's referenced in bug, chore, feature, patch, and prime. The planners read what your documenter just wrote.

**Checkpoint 4:** state the plan↔document cycle in one breath — document APPENDS the conditional entry; five planning prompts READ it; the next feature you plan pulls this doc only when its condition matches.

## 5 · Stretch drills (15–40 min, still zero hand-typing)

**S1 — The winning workflow.** Rerun the whole feature on a fresh issue with `adw_plan_build_test_review.py`. Note which phase catches your planted deviation — Dan: "the UI test very likely would have caught this... this is probably the winning workflow."
**S2 — Dan's named improvement (vision).** Via Claude Code, add "For every image you take, be sure to read it in during the review process" to `review.md`. Re-run `adw_review.py` on the same adw-id; compare `ReviewResult`s. Note where the fix does NOT belong: the global `.mcp.json --vision` ("this is outside of the ADW").
**S3 — Evals in practice.** Flip `/review` to a different model in `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP`, `git checkout` the pre-review state, rerun, diff the two review JSONs. You just built an eval from git.
**S4 — One-one-one census.** `ls agents/{adw_id}/` after a full run; map every agent folder to its single slash command and one purpose. Confirm no agent ran two prompts.
**S5 — Trigger-drift hunt.** From `classify_adw.md` vs `data_types.ADWWorkflow` / `workflow_ops.AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS`, prove why a webhook can never launch `adw_plan_build_review`. This is prompt↔code contract drift — exactly the failure class a review step exists to catch. (Optional: fix it via an `adw_patch` issue.)

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere — every change flowed through an ADW or Claude Code
- [ ] `agents/{adw_id}/adw_state.json` shows adw_id / issue_number / branch_name / plan_file / issue_class populated across phases
- [ ] Review posted a JSON-backed report with 1–5 screenshots and severity-classified issues
- [ ] You can state which severities block and what caps the resolution loop (3), no notes
- [ ] A patch plan exists under `specs/patch/` and its fix is visible in the app + PR
- [ ] An `app_docs/feature-*.md` exists with copied assets AND `conditional_docs.md` gained its entry **agentically**, not by hand
- [ ] Oral, no notes: five SDLC questions; testing-vs-review distinction; three constraints + which two the tactic bypasses; why compact is a band-aid; ideal presence count and its two moments

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall:** running `adw_review.py` / `adw_document.py` without the adw-id — they hard-exit demanding prior state. Remind students the ADW ID chains everything; copy it from the plan-phase output.
- **Second stall (Dan's own):** passing the PR number instead of the issue number to `adw_patch.py` (15 vs 14). Teach reading the state echo in the issue comments before blaming the tool.
- **"My screenshots are just file paths — it's broken."** No — the R2 uploader disables silently without the four Cloudflare vars. Local paths are the expected fallback; set the vars only if you want images to render on GitHub.
- **"Review passed but the button's wrong — the model failed."** Reframe it exactly as Dan does: blame the ADWs and skills, not the model. Two causes (test skipped; screenshots never read), one fix location (the review prompt). This is the lesson's most important teaching moment — don't let it slide into model-blaming.
- **Cost anxiety:** this lab spends more than TAC-1 (opus review + multiple full ADW runs). If the budget conversation surfaces, that IS the pay-to-play lesson arriving on schedule.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** webhook/cron out-loop triggering at scale, dangerous-mode production ADWs, the fleet-of-agents endgame — those are lesson 7+. Keep the five-question SDLC crisp and deflect scope creep.

# TAC-6 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)

TAC-6 ages well because its spine is primitives — the five SDLC questions, one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose, typed review contracts, conditional-doc feedback loops — and Dan pre-empts the churn on camera ("model intelligence is not a constraint"). But it's an Advanced lesson wired to a specific tooling moment, and seven things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.

---

## 1. One-purpose orchestration: hand-rolled `claude -p` processes → native subagents  ⟵ the big named gap

**Course era:** one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose is implemented as separate headless `claude -p` processes orchestrated by Python (`execute_template` → stream-json → per-agent folders). Works, and it's pedagogically perfect: nothing is hidden.
**Current:** Claude Code productizes the same tactic — subagents with their own context windows, tools, and system prompts (`.claude/agents/*.md`), spawnable in parallel from a main loop, plus background tasks. The rationale (fresh focused window per purpose) is unchanged and is now the OFFICIAL mental model for subagent design. External ADW-style orchestration still wins for deterministic CI/webhook pipelines; native subagents win for interactive fan-out.
**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. Teach the hand-rolled version first (you see every moving part), then show the same tactic as native subagents / Skills.
**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**) — the committed one-purpose prompt becomes a `SKILL.md`.

## 2. "Context pollution" → mainstream context engineering

**Course era:** Dan's vocabulary — context pollution / overloading / toxic context, the minimum context principle — predates the industry's "context engineering" wave, and the only lever shown is a fresh window per step.
**Current:** Claude Code adds machinery TAC-6 lacked: auto-compaction control, context editing, `/context` inspection, CLAUDE.md layering, and explicit long-session-degradation guidance. Dan's "compact is a band-aid — if your agent is compacting it is losing information" is now the consensus position, and the durable answer is still exactly what he teaches: fresh one-purpose contexts.
**Book treatment:** "current practice" callout naming the vocabulary alignment; no rewrite. The principle transfers unchanged.
**Overlay:** none required.

## 3. The screenshot-blind reviewer is solved tooling today

**Course era:** the lesson's sharpest self-critique — the review agent captures screenshots it never reads ("the tokens aren't flowing through the vision capabilities"), so a misplaced button sails through. Dan's fix is an in-prompt instruction to read every image.
**Current:** agents read images natively — Claude Code's Read renders PNGs into context, Playwright MCP has vision modes, computer-use agents screenshot-and-look by default. Dan's proposed one-liner is now standard practice.
**Book treatment:** teach the read-your-images instruction as the DEFAULT review-prompt line, not an optional improvement — but keep the whole failure story, because "blame the layer, encode the fix" is the transferable lesson, not the specific gap.
**Overlay:** none required.

## 4. R2 public bucket → one of several proof-hosting paths

**Course era:** review screenshots go to a public Cloudflare R2 bucket (S3-compatible boto3 + public domain, default `tac-public-imgs.iddagents.com`) so GitHub renders them inline.
**Current:** that path still works verbatim; alternatives now include `gh` CLI/API attachment uploads, inline images in PR review comments, CI-runner artifacts, and Agent SDK structured outputs carrying artifacts. The principle — proof lands IN the review system, publicly viewable, zero clicks to verify — transfers unchanged.
**Book treatment:** footnote listing the alternatives; keep R2 as the worked example.
**Overlay:** none required.

## 5. Model routing map: drifted names, now a first-class feature

**Course era:** `SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP` hardcodes `sonnet` / `opus` aliases (course-era Claude 4-class models) in a hand-rolled dict.
**Current:** the aliases still resolve, but current model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era) and per-agent `model:` frontmatter in subagent definitions make per-purpose model routing a supported feature, not a dict you maintain. The lesson's deeper insight — committed one-purpose prompts let you tune model/thinking per step and rerun as evals — is now also served by real eval harnesses and session resume/checkpointing.
**Book treatment:** margin note on the model-map frame ("aliases are period detail; per-purpose routing is now first-class"); teach the eval idea as durable.
**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **no** — already carried in phase 1 by TAC-1/TAC-3; volume-map reference only).

## 6. app_docs / ai_docs / specs → Dan's full 3-folder taxonomy

**Course era:** TAC-6 introduces `app_docs` (your codebase's docs) alongside `ai_docs` (third-party docs) and `specs` (plans), but the split gets one line: "AI docs for third party, app docs is for your codebase."
**Current:** Dan's public "3 codebase folders" treatment develops the taxonomy fully — the natural overlay for the documentation half of this lesson, including WHY conditional loading (not bulk loading) is the whole point.
**Book treatment:** overlay for the document / conditional-docs section.
**Overlay:** `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).

## 7. Repo drift: the two new composers are invisible to triggers (accuracy flag, not an ecosystem shift)

**Course era / on disk today:** `classify_adw.md` lists `/adw_plan_build_review` and `/adw_plan_build_document` as valid, but `data_types.ADWWorkflow` and `workflow_ops.AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS` omit both, so `extract_adw_info()` filters them out — webhook/cron classification can select every workflow EXCEPT those two composers. They're manual-entry-only.
**Book treatment:** carry it as a live worked example of prompt↔code contract drift — precisely the failure class a review step is supposed to catch. Not a dated feature; a permanent teaching artifact.
**Overlay:** none.

---

## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)

- One agent, one prompt, one purpose — more consensus now (native subagents) than at recording.
- Review ≠ testing. The two-question distinction is the load-bearing idea and is timeless.
- The typed review contract: strict JSON → pydantic `ReviewResult`, severity triage, blockers-only resolution, a hard retry cap, loud parse-failure.
- Severity triage for agreeable agents — skippable / tech_debt / blocker is templated judgment that still keeps nitpicks from blocking releases.
- The conditional-documentation feedback loop — document writes it, planners read it — is the lesson's crown jewel and has no expiry.
- The three constraints, and "model intelligence is not a constraint."
- "Compact is a band-aid." Truer now that we can actually measure context degradation.
- Minimum context principle; adopt your agent's perspective.
- Proof / the live-asset principle; review velocity; ideal presence = 2.
- Out-loop bias: fix the end-to-end portion, not the thing that went wrong. Blame the layer, not the model.
- Committed prompts become evals — git IS the eval infrastructure.

| 2 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | operationalizes tactic (the document half's home) | ✅ |
| 3 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (tool surface / SDK) — already in phase 1 elsewhere | ❌ defer |
| 4 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | fleet-of-agents endgame → lesson 7 (ZTE) | ❌ defer |

Exactly 2 included (within the 1–3 cap), matching `extract.json`.
